title: Native CSS Nesting
summary: Group related selectors inside a parent rule.

subtopics.title: Nest a related selector
subtopics.explanation: CSS nesting lets a related rule sit inside its parent rule. The outer selector describes the component; the inner selector describes a state or child. For example, a button rule can contain its hover rule. This keeps a small component’s styles together. Nest only when the relationship is easy to see, or a reader must trace too many levels to understand the final selector. Keep the rule close to its component when that relationship helps a teammate find it. If a selector targets a different component, move it to a separate top-level rule. A nested rule is like a note filed inside the folder it describes.

`&` stands for the parent selector. In `.button { &:hover { ... } }`, the browser matches a hovered button. It is like referring to the folder whose contents you are already editing. The ampersand can also combine classes and states, so inspect the resulting selector when syntax becomes complex. Use a separate rule when the target does not share the parent relationship. Write the resulting selector mentally or inspect it in browser tools. A misplaced ampersand can select a different relationship than the one intended.

subtopics.title: Nesting
subtopics.explanation: Native CSS nesting is understood by current browsers, but older targets may need a build transform. This is like using a shorthand that some readers need translated. Check the browser versions your product supports. Do not add a plugin just because nesting exists; use one only when the target browsers or project build require it. Browser support is a release constraint, not a syntax preference. Check the supported-browser policy and the production stylesheet before relying on an untransformed feature.

subtopics.title: Keep nesting shallow
subtopics.explanation: Keep nesting shallow, usually one level for a component state or child. Deep nesting creates long selectors that are difficult to override and test. For instance, nested card, header, icon, and hover rules can make one icon style depend on the whole markup tree. A simple class is often easier to maintain. Long chains make specificity harder to predict. A class on the target element often communicates the purpose more directly and permits simpler overrides. Keeping nesting shallow is like storing a tool where the next person expects to find it.

subtopics.title: Use nesting when it clarifies
subtopics.explanation: Use nesting when it makes the relationship clearer, not merely to reduce lines. Confirm the final selector in browser tools and check the production CSS if a build step transforms it. This helps catch an unexpected selector or specificity change before it reaches users. Build and test the same output users receive. Development tooling may transform CSS differently from a production pipeline. A build transform is like translating a new shorthand for an older reader.

foundations.overview: CSS nesting lets a stylesheet place a related rule inside its parent rule. This can keep component styles together, much like putting notes inside the folder they describe. Modern browsers support native nesting, but deeply nested rules become hard to follow and can create unexpectedly strong selectors. Use nesting for short, clear relationships and check the target browser support for the app.
foundations.whyItMatters: Nesting is a readability choice with browser-support and specificity consequences. Shallow, purposeful rules are easier to maintain than deeply nested structures.
foundations.realWorldUsage: It is like putting related notes under one heading.
commonUseCases: Group a button hover rule beside the button’s base rule.
Keep a component modifier near the component selector it changes.
Use a shallow nested rule for a small, clear state relationship.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Nesting always makes a stylesheet easier to read.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Deep nesting hides selector relationships and can create specificity that is difficult to override.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The ampersand is optional in every nested selector.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Its placement can change the resulting selector; inspect the browser support and final selector behavior.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Native nesting needs no support check.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Older target browsers may require a build transform, so match the syntax to the project’s browser policy.

keyTakeaways: CSS nesting lets a related rule sit inside its parent rule.
Native CSS nesting is understood by current browsers, but older targets may need a build transform.
Keep nesting shallow, usually one level for a component state or child.
Use nesting when it makes the relationship clearer, not merely to reduce lines.
